title: CSTM Technical Interview Questions
description: This assessment is designed to support revision and knowledge validation for candidates preparing for their CSTM technical interview. Note that these questions are asked in a 15 minute viva (interview) format in the actual exam.

questions.question: What is Root Squashing?

options.A: A Linux kernel hardening feature that disables all setuid binaries.
options.B: A DNS control that prevents zone transfers from unauthorized hosts.
options.C: A container isolation technique that forces root inside a container to map to root on the host.
options.D: An NFS feature that maps requests from the remote root user to an unprivileged user to prevent root-level access on the server.

questions.explanation: Root squashing is an NFS server feature that remaps requests from a remote root user (UID 0) to an unprivileged user (typically ‘nobody’), preventing a compromised or malicious NFS client with root access from gaining root-level read/write access to exported files on the server. It is not a kernel hardening feature (A), has nothing to do with DNS (B), and is the opposite of container UID mapping — it maps root to a non-root user, not to root on the host (C).

questions.question: Explain how run0 and the polkit can be used as a more secure alternative to sudo on Linux platforms.

options.A: They encrypt commands in transit so attackers cannot intercept sudo passwords over SSH.
options.B: They are used only for container escape prevention and do not relate to privilege elevation.
options.C: They allow fine-grained, policy-based privilege elevation for specific actions via polkit rules, reducing blanket shell access compared to broad sudo grants.
options.D: They replace PAM entirely and remove the need for authentication for administrative tasks.

questions.explanation: run0 is a systemd tool that uses polkit (PolicyKit) to request privilege elevation for specific actions rather than spawning a full root shell like sudo can. polkit uses declarative rules to grant fine-grained, per-action authorization, reducing the attack surface compared to broad sudoers entries. This is not about encrypting commands (A), not limited to container escapes (B), and does not replace PAM or remove authentication — it provides an alternative authorization path (D).

questions.question: What is DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance)?

options.A: A method for compressing email headers to reduce spam filtering overhead.
options.B: A DNS record type used to delegate subdomains securely to third parties.
options.C: An email authentication policy and reporting standard that builds on SPF and DKIM to help receivers handle spoofed mail and provide feedback reports.
options.D: A symmetric encryption protocol for securing SMTP sessions end-to-end.

questions.explanation: DMARC is a DNS-published email authentication policy that builds on SPF (sender IP authorization) and DKIM (cryptographic message signing) by adding alignment checks and a policy layer (none/quarantine/reject) that tells receivers how to handle mail that fails authentication. It also provides aggregate and forensic reporting so domain owners gain visibility into spoofing attempts. It does not compress headers (A), is not a delegation record (B), and is not an encryption protocol (D).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Sender Policy Framework (SPF)?

options.A: To sign outbound email content with a private key so recipients can validate integrity.
options.B: To encrypt email at rest on the recipient’s mail server.
options.C: To block all inbound mail that contains links or attachments.
options.D: To publish which mail servers are authorized to send email for a domain via DNS, helping prevent sender spoofing.

questions.explanation: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) works by publishing a DNS TXT record that lists the IP addresses and mail servers authorized to send email on behalf of a domain. Receiving mail servers check the envelope sender’s IP against this record and can reject or flag unauthorized sources, helping prevent email spoofing. SPF does not sign message content — that is DKIM (A). It does not encrypt email at rest (B) or block mail based on content (C).

questions.question: What is the purpose of DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)?

options.A: To enforce mandatory TLS between all mail relays on the internet.
options.B: To publish allowed sender IP ranges for a domain in DNS.
options.C: To prevent users from forwarding mail without breaking authentication.
options.D: To cryptographically sign email with a domain key so recipients can verify message integrity and that it was authorized by the domain.

questions.explanation: DKIM works by having the sending mail server cryptographically sign selected headers and the message body using a private key. The corresponding public key is published in a DNS TXT record. Recipients verify the DKIM-Signature header against this public key to confirm the message was authorized by the domain and was not tampered with in transit. It does not enforce TLS between relays (A) — that is MTA-STS/DANE. Publishing sender IP ranges is SPF (B). While forwarding can break DKIM, preventing forwarding is not its purpose (C).

questions.question: What are the security issues with the FTP protocol?

options.A: Credentials and data are typically transmitted in cleartext, making them vulnerable to interception and manipulation.
options.B: It is UDP-based and therefore cannot be filtered by firewalls.
options.C: It cannot support authentication, so anonymous access is mandatory.
options.D: It provides end-to-end encryption by default but is susceptible to key reuse.

questions.explanation: FTP transmits credentials (USER/PASS commands) and file data in cleartext over separate control (port 21) and data channels, making it vulnerable to network sniffing, credential theft, and man-in-the-middle attacks. Active mode FTP also introduces firewall complexity with dynamic data ports. FTP is TCP-based, not UDP (B), it does support authentication — anonymous access is optional (C), and it does not provide encryption by default (D). Secure alternatives include FTPS (FTP over TLS) and SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol).

questions.question: What is Kerberos?

options.A: A VPN tunneling protocol that encapsulates IP packets.
options.B: A password hashing scheme used by Windows to store credentials.
options.C: A public key infrastructure used to issue TLS certificates for web servers.
options.D: A ticket-based network authentication protocol that uses a trusted Key Distribution Center (KDC) to provide mutual authentication.

questions.explanation: Kerberos is a network authentication protocol that uses a trusted third party — the Key Distribution Center (KDC), comprising an Authentication Server (AS) and Ticket Granting Server (TGS) — to issue time-limited tickets. Users authenticate once to obtain a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT), then use it to request service tickets for specific resources without resending their password. This provides mutual authentication and is the default authentication protocol in Active Directory. It is not a VPN protocol (A), not a password hashing scheme (B), and not a PKI for TLS certificates (C).

questions.question: Explain directory traversal exploitation

options.A: Injecting SQL meta-characters to extract database rows.
options.B: Manipulating path input (e.g., ../) to access files outside the intended directory, potentially reading sensitive files or executing unintended resources.
options.C: Abusing DNS recursion to enumerate internal hosts.
options.D: Forcing the application to reuse a session token created by another user.

questions.explanation: Directory traversal (also called path traversal) exploits occur when an application uses user-supplied input to construct file paths without proper validation or sanitization. Attackers use sequences like '../' or encoded variants to escape the intended directory and access arbitrary files on the server, such as /etc/passwd, configuration files, or application source code. This is distinct from SQL injection (A), DNS enumeration (C), or session fixation (D). Mitigations include input validation, path canonicalization, chroot jails, and avoiding direct use of user input in file operations.

questions.question: What are the four types of Application Programming Interface (API)?

options.A: REST, SOAP, RPC, and GraphQL.
options.B: TCP, UDP, ICMP, and ARP.
options.C: SQL, NoSQL, LDAP, and SMB.
options.D: Public (open), Partner, Private (internal), and Composite APIs.

questions.explanation: APIs are commonly classified by their exposure and composition: Public (open) APIs are available to external developers; Partner APIs are shared with specific business partners under agreements; Private (internal) APIs are used within an organization; and Composite APIs combine multiple API calls into a single request for efficiency. Option A (REST, SOAP, RPC, GraphQL) describes API architectural styles/paradigms, not the four types by access level. Options B and C list network and storage protocols, not API types.

questions.question: How would you fingerprint a database server?

options.A: Only by cracking the database administrator password and logging in.
options.B: By checking the web server’s TLS certificate issuer.
options.C: By using ARP spoofing to force the server to reveal its database type.
options.D: Enumerate banners/version via service probes, review error messages and protocol responses, and validate with authenticated queries where permitted.

questions.explanation: Database fingerprinting uses multiple techniques: service probes (e.g., nmap scripts) to identify listening ports and banners, analyzing error messages that reveal DB type and version (e.g., MySQL vs PostgreSQL vs MSSQL error formats), examining protocol-specific responses, and — where authorized — running version queries (e.g., SELECT @@version). This multi-layered approach is more reliable than any single method. You do not need to crack credentials first (A), TLS certificate issuers do not identify databases (B), and ARP spoofing is a network-layer attack unrelated to DB identification (C).

questions.question: Explain symmetrical and asymmetrical cryptography

options.A: They are identical; the terms refer to different cipher modes.
options.B: Symmetric uses public keys only; asymmetric uses passwords only.
options.C: Symmetric uses the same key for encryption/decryption; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair for encryption, signatures, and key exchange.
options.D: Symmetric is slower and used only for signatures; asymmetric is faster and used for bulk data.

questions.explanation: Symmetric cryptography uses a single shared secret key for both encryption and decryption (e.g., AES, ChaCha20), making it fast and suitable for bulk data encryption. Asymmetric cryptography uses a mathematically linked key pair — a public key (shared openly) and a private key (kept secret) — enabling encryption, digital signatures, and secure key exchange without prior shared secrets (e.g., RSA, ECDH). The terms are not identical (A), the key usage is the opposite of B, and symmetric is actually faster than asymmetric — not slower (D). Most real-world protocols (e.g., TLS) use both in a hybrid approach.

questions.question: What is the difference between SQL and no SQL database vulnerabilities?

options.A: NoSQL vulnerabilities only relate to buffer overflows in the kernel.
options.B: SQL systems commonly face SQL injection via query concatenation; NoSQL can face NoSQL injection through unvalidated query objects/operators and may differ in auth/ACL models.
options.C: SQL databases cannot be attacked remotely because they only run locally.
options.D: NoSQL databases are immune to injection attacks by design.

questions.explanation: SQL databases are vulnerable to SQL injection where attackers manipulate structured query language through string concatenation. NoSQL databases (e.g., MongoDB, CouchDB) face different injection vectors — such as JSON/BSON operator injection (e.g., $gt, $ne operators), JavaScript injection in server-side evaluation, or manipulating query objects. NoSQL databases may also have weaker default authentication and access control models compared to mature SQL platforms. NoSQL is not limited to buffer overflows (A), SQL databases can absolutely be attacked remotely (C), and NoSQL databases are not immune to injection — they just have different attack surfaces (D).

questions.question: What is the Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL)?

options.A: A protocol for securely transporting vulnerability scan results over TLS.
options.B: A penetration testing methodology framework for web applications.
options.C: A vulnerability scoring system that replaces CVSS.
options.D: A standard for representing and exchanging security configuration and vulnerability checks in a machine-readable way.

questions.explanation: OVAL is an XML-based standard maintained by MITRE/CIS that provides a machine-readable language for expressing system configuration checks and vulnerability assessments. It defines definitions, tests, objects, and states that security tools can use to consistently evaluate system posture. It is not a transport protocol (A), not a pen testing methodology like OWASP or PTES (B), and does not replace CVSS — CVSS scores severity while OVAL describes how to detect vulnerabilities (C).

questions.question: Explain the difference between Phishing, Smishing and Vishing and what risks do they pose?

options.A: They are all technical exploits with no user interaction required.
options.B: Smishing is email-based and phishing is SMS-based; vishing is social media-based.
options.C: Phishing is only for credential theft; smishing is only for malware; vishing is only for DDoS.
options.D: Phishing uses email, smishing uses SMS/messages, and vishing uses voice calls; all aim to trick users into revealing data, installing malware, or authorizing fraud.

questions.explanation: These are three distinct social engineering delivery channels: Phishing uses email (e.g., fake login pages, malicious attachments), Smishing uses SMS/text messages (e.g., fraudulent links sent to phones), and Vishing uses voice calls (e.g., impersonating banks or IT support). All aim to trick victims into revealing credentials, authorizing transactions, or installing malware. They require user interaction — they are not technical exploits (A). Option B reverses the definitions of phishing and smishing. Each channel can be used for any of these attack goals, not just one specific purpose each (C).

questions.question: What tools could you use to enumerate Domain Name System (DNS) for ZONE transfer vulnerabilities?

options.A: tcpdump and Wireshark only; DNS cannot be queried directly.
options.B: dig, nslookup, and specialized tools like dnsrecon or fierce to attempt AXFR against authoritative name servers.
options.C: hashcat and john; zone transfers require password cracking.
options.D: nmap only; DNS servers do not support zone transfers.

questions.explanation: DNS zone transfer (AXFR) vulnerabilities are tested using tools like 'dig axfr @nameserver domain.com' or 'nslookup' with 'ls -d domain'. Specialized tools like dnsrecon, fierce, and dnsenum automate the process of identifying authoritative name servers and attempting zone transfers to reveal all DNS records for a domain. A successful zone transfer exposes the full DNS zone including internal hostnames, IP addresses, and network topology. Wireshark captures traffic but does not query DNS directly (A), zone transfers do not require password cracking (C), and nmap alone is insufficient — though its dns-zone-transfer NSE script can help (D).

questions.question: Explain what a Security identifier (SID) is and the different parts of a SID.

options.A: A Windows identifier for users/groups: revision, identifier authority, and one or more subauthorities (including domain SID and RID).
options.B: A Linux file permission string made of owner/group/other bits.
options.C: A Kerberos ticket field that stores session keys and timestamps.
options.D: A DNS record that maps hostnames to IPv4 addresses.

questions.explanation: A Security Identifier (SID) is a unique value used in Windows to identify security principals (users, groups, computers). Its structure includes: a revision level (S-1), an identifier authority (e.g., 5 for NT Authority), subauthority values identifying the domain, and a Relative Identifier (RID) as the final component (e.g., 500 for Administrator, 501 for Guest). For example, S-1-5-21-<domain>-500 identifies the built-in Administrator. SIDs are a Windows concept, not Linux file permissions (B), not Kerberos ticket fields (C), and not DNS records (D).

questions.question: What are the two IPsec encoding methods and what are the pros and cons of each?

options.A: RSA and AES; RSA is slower but more secure than AES.
options.B: Transport mode (protects payload; less overhead) and Tunnel mode (encapsulates entire IP packet; better for gateway-to-gateway/VPNs but more overhead).
options.C: Cleartext and Encrypted; cleartext is faster but equally secure.
options.D: Base64 and Hex; Base64 is smaller but less secure than Hex.

questions.explanation: IPsec has two encoding modes: Transport mode encrypts/authenticates only the IP payload while preserving the original IP header, making it efficient for host-to-host communication with less overhead. Tunnel mode encapsulates the entire original IP packet inside a new IP packet, providing full protection including the original headers — ideal for site-to-site VPNs and gateway-to-gateway traffic but with additional overhead. RSA and AES are algorithms, not IPsec modes (A). Cleartext is not an IPsec mode (C). Base64 and Hex are encoding formats unrelated to IPsec (D).

questions.question: In key signing do you use the private or public key for signing?

options.A: The public key is used to sign; the private key is used to verify.
options.B: Both keys must be combined to sign a message.
options.C: The private key is used to create the signature; the public key is used to verify it.
options.D: Neither key is used; signing uses only hashing.

questions.explanation: In digital signing, the signer uses their private key to create a signature over a hash of the message. Anyone with access to the signer’s public key can verify the signature, confirming both the signer’s identity (authentication) and that the message was not altered (integrity). This also provides non-repudiation since only the private key holder could have created the signature. The roles are reversed in option A. Both keys are not combined (B) — each has a distinct role. Hashing alone cannot produce a verifiable signature without a key pair (D).

questions.question: What ports need to be open on a domain controller (DC)?

options.A: Only TCP 22 for SSH administration.
options.B: Only TCP 80 and 443 for web-based authentication.
options.C: Only UDP 161 for SNMP monitoring.
options.D: Core services include Kerberos (88), LDAP (389/636), DNS (53), SMB/RPC (445 plus RPC dynamic ports), and often Global Catalog (3268/3269).

questions.explanation: A Windows domain controller runs multiple critical services requiring numerous ports: Kerberos authentication (TCP/UDP 88), LDAP (TCP/UDP 389) and LDAPS (TCP 636), DNS (TCP/UDP 53), SMB (TCP 445), RPC endpoint mapper (TCP 135) plus dynamic RPC ports, Global Catalog (TCP 3268/3269), and NTP (UDP 123) among others. The exact list depends on services enabled and topology (e.g., replication, DFSR). DCs do not use SSH (A), are not web-only services (B), and SNMP alone is insufficient for DC operations (C).

questions.question: Explain the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) protocol and any weaknesses in the protocol

options.A: SNMP is used only for email routing and is encrypted by default.
options.B: SNMP cannot be queried remotely, so it has no practical weaknesses.
options.C: SNMP is for monitoring/management; weaknesses include plaintext community strings in v1/v2c and weak/default credentials; v3 improves with auth/privacy but can be misconfigured.
options.D: SNMP is a file transfer protocol with no authentication.

questions.explanation: SNMP is used for monitoring and managing network devices (routers, switches, servers). SNMPv1 and v2c transmit community strings (essentially passwords) in cleartext, and default strings like 'public' (read) and 'private' (read-write) are frequently left unchanged, allowing attackers to enumerate device configurations or even modify settings. SNMPv3 improves security by adding authentication (e.g., HMAC-SHA) and encryption (e.g., AES) for privacy, but misconfiguration, weak credentials, or fallback to v2c can negate these protections. SNMP is not for email routing (A), it can be queried remotely — that is its purpose (B), and it is not a file transfer protocol (D).

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between symmetrical and asymmetrical cryptography?

options.A: Symmetric is fast for bulk encryption but requires secure key sharing; asymmetric simplifies key distribution and supports signatures but is slower and used mainly for key exchange/authentication.
options.B: Asymmetric is always faster and preferred for encrypting large files.
options.C: There are no trade-offs; both have identical performance and properties.
options.D: Symmetric provides non-repudiation; asymmetric does not.

questions.explanation: Symmetric encryption (e.g., AES) is computationally fast and efficient for encrypting large amounts of data, but requires both parties to securely share the same secret key — a significant challenge at scale (the key distribution problem). Asymmetric encryption (e.g., RSA, ECDH) solves key distribution by using public/private key pairs, enabling secure key exchange and digital signatures, but is much slower and impractical for bulk data. In practice, hybrid cryptosystems (like TLS) use asymmetric cryptography for the initial handshake and key exchange, then switch to symmetric encryption for the data session. Asymmetric is not faster (B), there are clear trade-offs (C), and it is asymmetric — not symmetric — that provides non-repudiation via digital signatures (D).

questions.question: Explain some vulnerabilities in SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and TLS (Transport Layer Security)?

options.A: The only vulnerability is that TLS cannot support perfect forward secrecy.
options.B: SSL/TLS vulnerabilities only occur at the IP layer, not the application layer.
options.C: TLS is immune to misconfiguration because it auto-selects the best cipher.
options.D: Examples include obsolete protocol versions (SSLv2/v3), weak ciphers, downgrade attacks, poor certificate validation, and implementation bugs (e.g., Heartbleed).

questions.explanation: SSL/TLS vulnerabilities span multiple categories: obsolete protocols (SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1) with known weaknesses like POODLE and BEAST; weak cipher suites (RC4, DES, export ciphers); downgrade attacks (FREAK, Logjam) that force weaker cryptography; implementation bugs (Heartbleed in OpenSSL, which leaked server memory); and poor certificate validation enabling MITM attacks. Modern best practice mandates TLS 1.2+ (preferably 1.3), strong cipher suites with PFS, proper certificate chain validation, and HSTS. TLS 1.3 does support PFS by design (A), vulnerabilities affect the transport layer not just IP (B), and TLS does not auto-select the best cipher without proper configuration (C).

questions.question: Explain the purpose of a Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) server

options.A: To host web applications behind a reverse proxy.
options.B: To perform DNS zone transfers between authoritative servers.
options.C: To provide centralized AAA (authentication, authorization, accounting) for network access such as VPN, Wi-Fi (802.1X), and dial-in services.
options.D: To encrypt all LAN traffic at Layer 2.

questions.explanation: RADIUS provides centralized Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) for network access. It authenticates users connecting via VPN, Wi-Fi (802.1X), dial-in, or wired 802.1X by proxying credentials to a backend (e.g., Active Directory). It authorizes what resources/VLANs the user can access, and accounts for session usage (time, data transferred). Network devices (access points, switches, VPN gateways) act as RADIUS clients that forward access requests to the RADIUS server. It is not a reverse proxy (A), has nothing to do with DNS zone transfers (B), and does not encrypt LAN traffic at Layer 2 (D).

questions.question: Where are passwords stored on server devices?

options.A: Typically as salted hashes in OS-specific stores (e.g., /etc/shadow on Linux; SAM/NTDS.dit for Windows), not as reversible plaintext.
options.B: Only in DNS TXT records for the domain.
options.C: Only inside the BIOS/UEFI firmware on the motherboard.
options.D: Always in plaintext in /etc/passwd on Linux.

questions.explanation: On Linux, password hashes are stored in /etc/shadow (readable only by root), using algorithms like SHA-512 or yescrypt with per-user salts. The /etc/passwd file contains user account information but not the actual password hashes on modern systems. On Windows, local password hashes (NTLM) are stored in the SAM (Security Account Manager) database, and domain credentials are stored in NTDS.dit on domain controllers. Both are protected by OS access controls. Passwords are not stored in DNS (B), not in BIOS/UEFI (C), and modern Linux does not store passwords in plaintext in /etc/passwd (D) — that practice ended decades ago with the move to /etc/shadow.

questions.question: Explain Structured Query Language injection (SQLi)

options.A: A technique to overflow the stack by sending long SQL strings.
options.B: A DNS attack that injects records into a resolver cache.
options.C: A method to bypass TLS encryption by injecting SQL keywords.
options.D: An attack where untrusted input is concatenated into SQL queries, allowing attackers to alter query logic to read/modify data or execute database functions.

questions.explanation: SQL injection occurs when user-supplied input is concatenated directly into SQL queries without proper sanitization or parameterization. Attackers can inject SQL syntax (e.g., ' OR 1=1 --) to bypass authentication, extract data (UNION-based), modify/delete records, or in some cases execute OS commands via functions like xp_cmdshell. Types include in-band (error-based, UNION-based), blind (boolean-based, time-based), and out-of-band SQLi. The primary mitigation is parameterized queries/prepared statements, which separate SQL code from data. It is not a stack overflow attack (A), not related to DNS (B), and not related to TLS (C).

questions.question: If password hashes cannot be cracked can the hashes be used in any way and how would you do this?

options.A: Yes—upload hashes to DNS to gain domain admin automatically.
options.B: Yes—convert the hash into an AES key and decrypt any file on the network.
options.C: No—hashes are useless unless cracked into plaintext.
options.D: Yes—Pass-the-Hash (and related token-based abuses) can authenticate using the hash directly (e.g., NTLM) without recovering the plaintext password.

questions.explanation: Pass-the-Hash (PtH) is an attack technique where an attacker uses a captured NTLM password hash to authenticate to remote services without needing to crack it to plaintext. This works because the NTLM protocol uses the hash directly as the authenticating credential in the challenge-response mechanism. Tools like Mimikatz, CrackMapExec, and Impacket's psexec/wmiexec can perform PtH attacks. Related techniques include Pass-the-Ticket (Kerberos) and overpass-the-hash. Mitigations include disabling NTLM where possible, using Kerberos, implementing credential guard, enforcing least privilege, and deploying MFA. Hashes cannot be uploaded to DNS (A) or converted to AES keys (B), and hashes are definitely not useless if uncracked (C).

questions.question: Explain how a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) exploit works

options.A: It exploits SQL injection to modify database rows directly.
options.B: It tricks an authenticated user’s browser into submitting a state-changing request to a trusted site, leveraging existing session cookies.
options.C: It forces a server to accept malformed TLS certificates.
options.D: It steals passwords by keylogging the user’s keyboard in the browser.

questions.explanation: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic inclusion of cookies (session cookies, authentication tokens) when making requests to a site. An attacker crafts a malicious page or link that triggers a state-changing request (e.g., changing an email address, transferring funds) to a trusted site where the victim is already authenticated. The victim's browser automatically attaches valid session cookies, making the forged request appear legitimate. Mitigations include anti-CSRF tokens (synchronizer tokens), SameSite cookie attributes, checking the Origin/Referer header, and requiring re-authentication for sensitive actions. CSRF is distinct from SQL injection (A), does not involve TLS certificates (C), and is not a keylogger (D).

questions.question: Explain session hijacking (with respect to web application testing)

options.A: Brute forcing a database admin account until access is granted.
options.B: Forcing a VPN tunnel to renegotiate encryption keys.
options.C: Taking over a valid user session by stealing or predicting session tokens (e.g., via XSS, sniffing, or insecure cookies) and reusing them to impersonate the user.
options.D: Exploiting directory traversal to read server-side source code.

questions.explanation: Session hijacking involves an attacker obtaining or predicting a valid session token to impersonate an authenticated user. Attack vectors include: XSS to steal cookies via JavaScript, network sniffing on unencrypted connections, session fixation (forcing a known session ID), brute-forcing weak/predictable session IDs, and accessing tokens from logs or referrer headers. Once the attacker has the session token, they can replay it to access the application as the victim. Mitigations include using HTTPS everywhere, setting Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite cookie flags, regenerating session IDs after login, implementing session timeouts, and preventing XSS. It is not database brute forcing (A), VPN key renegotiation (B), or directory traversal (D).

questions.question: What is Internet Information Service (IIS)?

options.A: A Linux init system for starting services.
options.B: A VPN protocol for site-to-site tunneling.
options.C: A database engine used for NoSQL document storage.
options.D: Microsoft’s web server platform for hosting websites and web applications on Windows.

questions.explanation: Internet Information Services (IIS) is Microsoft's web server software built into Windows Server. It supports hosting websites and web applications using HTTP/HTTPS, with features including application pools for process isolation, integrated Windows authentication (NTLM/Kerberos), support for ASP.NET and .NET Core, URL rewriting, request filtering, and centralized certificate management. IIS is commonly found in enterprise environments and is a frequent target during penetration tests. It is not a Linux init system (A), not a VPN protocol (B), and not a database engine (C).

questions.question: Explain baseboard management controller (BMC) Hacking and the Intelligent Platform Management Interface (IPMI)

options.A: Hacking the GPU driver to increase rendering performance.
options.B: Using ARP spoofing to intercept DNS queries on the LAN.
options.C: Attacking out-of-band management interfaces (e.g., IPMI/BMC) to gain hardware-level control, often via weak auth, default creds, exposed services, or firmware flaws.
options.D: Abusing SMTP relays to send unauthenticated email.

questions.explanation: The Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) is an embedded microcontroller on server motherboards that provides out-of-band management via the Intelligent Platform Management Interface (IPMI). It enables remote power control, KVM console access, hardware monitoring, and firmware updates — even when the main OS is powered off. Security issues include: IPMI v2.0 RAKP allowing password hash extraction without authentication, default/weak credentials (e.g., ADMIN/ADMIN on many vendors), plaintext IPMI v1.5, exposed web interfaces with known CVEs, and firmware vulnerabilities. Compromise gives an attacker hardware-level persistent access below the OS layer. BMC/IPMI management interfaces should be isolated on a dedicated management VLAN with strict ACLs. It is unrelated to GPU drivers (A), ARP spoofing (B), or SMTP relays (D).

questions.question: What are the pros and cons of using the cloud vs on prem (in terms of cyber security)?

options.A: Cloud removes the need for identity management entirely.
options.B: On-prem eliminates insider threats; cloud increases them only.
options.C: Cloud can offer strong baseline controls and rapid patching, but introduces shared-responsibility, misconfiguration risk, and dependency on provider controls; on-prem offers direct control but requires in-house security maturity.
options.D: Cloud is always less secure because it is public; on-prem is always secure.

questions.explanation: Cloud environments offer strong baseline security controls (provider-managed physical security, rapid patching, built-in redundancy, advanced DDoS protection), but introduce the shared responsibility model where the customer must correctly configure IAM, networking, storage, and encryption. Misconfiguration (e.g., public S3 buckets, overly permissive security groups) is a leading cause of cloud breaches. On-premises provides direct physical and logical control but demands significant in-house security expertise, patch management, and infrastructure investment. Cloud does not eliminate identity management (A), on-prem does not eliminate insider threats (B), and neither environment is inherently always more or less secure than the other (D).

questions.question: What technical controls are available in the cloud to help with cyber security?

options.A: Only DNS filtering; other controls are not available.
options.B: IAM policies/MFA, network segmentation (VPC/VNet, security groups), logging/monitoring, encryption/KMS, WAF/DDoS protections, and posture management tools.
options.C: Only physical security at the data center perimeter.
options.D: Only antivirus installed on virtual machines.

questions.explanation: Cloud providers offer a comprehensive suite of security controls: IAM policies with MFA and least-privilege access; network segmentation via VPCs/VNets, security groups, and NACLs; centralized logging and monitoring (e.g., CloudTrail, Azure Monitor, GCP Cloud Audit Logs); encryption at rest and in transit with managed key services (KMS); WAF and DDoS protection services (e.g., AWS Shield, Azure DDoS Protection); and cloud security posture management (CSPM) tools for detecting misconfigurations. These controls require proper configuration and ongoing governance to be effective. Cloud security is not limited to just DNS filtering (A), physical security alone (C), or antivirus (D).

questions.question: What are the most popular containerization solutions?

options.A: Docker and containerd, often orchestrated with Kubernetes; podman is also common as a daemonless alternative.
options.B: Hyper-V and VMware ESXi.
options.C: WEP and WPA2.
options.D: SMTP and IMAP.

questions.explanation: Docker is the most widely recognized containerization platform, using containerd as its underlying container runtime. Podman is a popular daemonless alternative that runs containers without a central daemon process, improving security. Kubernetes (K8s) is the dominant container orchestration platform for managing deployment, scaling, and networking of containerized workloads. These solutions all use OCI (Open Container Initiative) compatible images and runtimes. Hyper-V and VMware ESXi are hypervisors for virtual machines, not containers (B). WEP and WPA2 are wireless security protocols (C). SMTP and IMAP are email protocols (D).

questions.question: What’s the difference between virtual machines and containerization?

options.A: VMs cannot be networked; containers can.
options.B: VMs virtualize hardware and run separate OS kernels; containers share the host kernel and isolate processes, making them lighter but with different isolation boundaries.
options.C: Containers are always more secure because they cannot escape.
options.D: Containers require a hypervisor; VMs run directly on the host kernel.

questions.explanation: Virtual machines use a hypervisor to virtualize hardware, running a complete guest OS with its own kernel on top, providing strong isolation boundaries. Containers share the host OS kernel and use kernel features (namespaces, cgroups, seccomp) to isolate processes, making them lighter, faster to start, and more resource-efficient, but with a thinner isolation boundary — a kernel exploit could affect all containers. VMs can be networked (A is false). Containers can escape under certain conditions, so they are not inherently always more secure (C). Containers do not require a hypervisor — they run on the host kernel; VMs require hypervisors (D reverses this).

questions.question: What are the signs a mobile device has been jail broken?

options.A: The screen brightness increases automatically at night.
options.B: Presence of root/jailbreak tools (e.g., Cydia/Sileo), unusual privilege escalation apps, disabled sandboxing indicators, or integrity checks failing (e.g., SafetyNet/DeviceCheck).
options.C: The device can connect to Wi‑Fi networks.
options.D: The phone battery lasts longer than normal.

questions.explanation: Signs of a jailbroken/rooted device include: presence of jailbreak tools like Cydia or Sileo (iOS) or Magisk/SuperSU (Android); apps with root/su binary access; modified system partitions or boot images; failing platform integrity checks such as Android's Play Integrity API (formerly SafetyNet) or Apple's DeviceCheck/App Attest; the ability to install apps from unofficial sources; and SSH servers running on non-standard ports. These indicators can be detected by MDM solutions and security applications. Increased screen brightness (A) and Wi-Fi connectivity (C) are normal device behavior. Jailbroken devices typically have worse battery life, not better (D).

questions.question: What file types are associated with android apps?

options.A: APK (and the newer AAB for Play distribution), with DEX bytecode inside packages.
options.B: EXE and MSI.
options.C: JAR only; Android does not use packages.
options.D: IPA and DMG.

questions.explanation: Android applications are packaged as APK (Android Package Kit) files — ZIP archives containing DEX bytecode (compiled Java/Kotlin), resources, assets, the AndroidManifest.xml, and native libraries. Google Play now requires AAB (Android App Bundle) format for submission, which Google Play processes to generate optimized APKs for each device configuration. Inside APKs, the compiled code runs as DEX (Dalvik Executable) bytecode on the ART runtime. EXE/MSI are Windows formats (B), JAR files are generic Java archives and Android does not use them directly (C), and IPA/DMG are Apple formats (D).

questions.question: What file types are associated with apple apps?

options.A: RPM and DEB.
options.B: IPA packages (iOS/iPadOS), and macOS apps commonly as .app bundles or distributed via DMG/PKG installers.
options.C: EXE and BAT.
options.D: APK and AAB.

questions.explanation: iOS and iPadOS apps are distributed as IPA (iOS App Store Package) files — ZIP archives containing the compiled app binary, resources, and code signature. macOS applications are typically .app bundles (directory structures containing the executable, frameworks, and resources), distributed via DMG (disk image) or PKG (installer package) files, or through the Mac App Store. All Apple apps must be code-signed and, for App Store distribution, notarized by Apple. RPM/DEB are Linux package formats (A), EXE/BAT are Windows formats (C), and APK/AAB are Android formats (D).

questions.question: Explain the use case for Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS).

options.A: To provide TLS-like encryption and authentication over UDP for latency-sensitive applications (e.g., VoIP, WebRTC) where TCP is unsuitable.
options.B: To compress UDP payloads to improve throughput.
options.C: To route DNS queries anonymously through relays.
options.D: To replace IPsec for encrypting disks at rest.

questions.explanation: DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security) adapts the TLS protocol to work over UDP and other datagram transports. Since UDP is connectionless and does not guarantee ordering or delivery, DTLS adds its own sequence numbers, retransmission timers, and replay protection while providing the same encryption, authentication, and integrity guarantees as TLS. Key use cases include WebRTC (real-time browser communication), VoIP, video conferencing, VPN protocols (e.g., Cisco AnyConnect, OpenConnect), and IoT protocols like CoAP. It does not compress payloads (B), is not related to DNS anonymization (C), and is not a disk encryption replacement for IPsec (D).

questions.question: What are the built-in user accounts on a Windows server?

options.A: postgres, mysql, and sa.
options.B: ec2-user and ubuntu.
options.C: Common built-ins include Administrator, Guest (often disabled), and service accounts like LocalSystem, LocalService, and NetworkService.
options.D: root, nobody, and daemon.

questions.explanation: Windows Server includes several built-in accounts: the Administrator account (SID ending in -500, full local admin access), the Guest account (typically disabled by default, limited access), and service accounts including LocalSystem (highest privilege, acts as the computer on the network), LocalService (limited local privilege, anonymous network access), and NetworkService (limited local privilege, authenticates to the network as the machine account). Active Directory domain controllers also include KRBTGT for Kerberos ticket encryption. Hardening involves disabling Guest, renaming Administrator, and applying least privilege. Options A (database accounts), B (cloud Linux AMI users), and D (Unix/Linux accounts) are for other operating systems.

questions.question: Name some protocols in the Industrial control system (ICS) / Operational Technology (OT) space?

options.A: IMAP, POP3, and SMTP only.
options.B: SIP, RTP, and SRTP only.
options.C: BGP, OSPF, and IS-IS only.
options.D: Modbus, DNP3, BACnet, OPC (classic/UA), and PROFINET are common ICS/OT protocols.

questions.explanation: Common ICS/OT protocols include: Modbus (serial/TCP, widely used for SCADA with no built-in authentication), DNP3 (Distributed Network Protocol, used in utilities for SCADA communication), BACnet (Building Automation and Control Networks), OPC Classic (COM/DCOM-based) and OPC UA (modern, platform-independent with security features), and PROFINET (industrial Ethernet for automation). Many of these protocols were designed for isolated networks and lack authentication, encryption, or integrity checking, making them vulnerable when exposed to IP networks. IMAP/POP3/SMTP are email protocols (A), SIP/RTP are VoIP protocols (B), and BGP/OSPF/IS-IS are IP routing protocols (C).

questions.question: Name some security models and what is the purpose of security models?

options.A: Examples include Bell–LaPadula, Biba, Clark–Wilson, and Brewer–Nash; they formalize security properties and guide system policy/design.
options.B: Examples include RAID levels; they define disk redundancy.
options.C: Examples include TCP/IP and OSI; they define packet formats.
options.D: Examples include AES and RSA; they define encryption algorithms.

questions.explanation: Security models are formal frameworks that define rules and properties for enforcing security policies: Bell-LaPadula enforces confidentiality ('no read up, no write down'), Biba enforces integrity ('no read down, no write up'), Clark-Wilson provides integrity through well-formed transactions and separation of duties, and Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall) prevents conflicts of interest by dynamically restricting access. These models guide system design and policy enforcement, providing mathematical assurance about security properties. RAID levels relate to disk redundancy (B), TCP/IP and OSI are networking models (C), and AES/RSA are cryptographic algorithms, not security models (D).

questions.question: What are the issues with the Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) protocol?

options.A: It uses weak IVs and RC4 key scheduling, enabling practical key recovery and traffic decryption; it is considered broken.
options.B: It mandates AES-256 and therefore is too slow for Wi‑Fi.
options.C: It cannot authenticate clients, so all Wi‑Fi is anonymous.
options.D: It is immune to replay attacks due to perfect forward secrecy.

questions.explanation: WEP uses RC4 stream cipher with 24-bit Initialization Vectors (IVs) that are transmitted in cleartext and repeat frequently on busy networks. The weak IV scheduling (FMS attack) and related attacks (PTW, chopchop, fragmentation) allow an attacker to recover the WEP key from passively captured traffic in minutes using tools like aircrack-ng. WEP also lacks proper integrity protection (CRC32 is not cryptographically secure) and has no protection against replay attacks. WEP does not use AES-256 (B), it does support authentication via shared key or open system (C), and it has no forward secrecy at all (D). WPA2 (AES-CCMP) or WPA3 (SAE) should always be used instead.

questions.question: What are the security issues associated with Lanman (LM) passwords?

options.A: They require smart cards, which are easy to clone.
options.B: They store plaintext passwords in the registry by default.
options.C: They are case-insensitive, split into 7-character chunks, and use weak hashing, making them highly susceptible to brute force and rainbow tables.
options.D: They are salted with modern bcrypt, making cracking infeasible.

questions.explanation: LanMan (LM) hashes have critical weaknesses: passwords are converted to uppercase (eliminating case as an entropy factor), truncated or padded to 14 characters, then split into two independent 7-character halves that are each used as a DES key to encrypt a fixed string. This means each 7-character half can be cracked independently, dramatically reducing the keyspace. Combined with no salting, LM hashes are extremely vulnerable to rainbow table and brute-force attacks — a full LM hash can typically be cracked in minutes. LM hashes do not use smart cards (A), do not store plaintext (B), and definitely do not use bcrypt (D). Modern Windows systems should disable LM hash storage via Group Policy.

questions.question: Explain the purpose of the phpMyAdmin application.

options.A: A VPN client for IPsec tunnels.
options.B: A Linux kernel module for memory management.
options.C: A web-based administration interface for MySQL/MariaDB to manage databases, users, and queries.
options.D: A Windows service for domain authentication.

questions.explanation: phpMyAdmin is an open-source PHP web application that provides a graphical interface for managing MySQL and MariaDB databases. It allows administrators to create/modify databases and tables, run SQL queries, manage users and permissions, import/export data, and browse table contents through a web browser. From a security perspective, phpMyAdmin is a high-value target because it provides direct database access — it should be restricted by IP, placed behind authentication, kept updated, and ideally not exposed to the public internet. It is not a VPN client (A), not a kernel module (B), and not a Windows authentication service (D).

questions.question: How would you find and download files from a File Transfer Protocol (FTP) server or a Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server?

options.A: By querying DNS TXT records for file contents.
options.B: Only by exploiting buffer overflows in the FTP server.
options.C: Enumerate directories/files (e.g., ftp ls/dir; nmap scripts), then retrieve with ftp get/mget or tftp get, respecting authorization and scope.
options.D: By sending ICMP echo requests and reading the payload.

questions.explanation: For FTP: connect using an FTP client, authenticate (or use anonymous if allowed), list directories with 'ls' or 'dir', and retrieve files with 'get' or 'mget'. Nmap scripts (e.g., ftp-anon, ftp-bounce) can identify anonymous access and enumerate content. For TFTP: since it has no authentication or directory listing capability, you typically need to know filenames and retrieve them with 'tftp -g' or 'atftp'. TFTP commonly runs on UDP port 69 and is often used for firmware/config file transfers on internal networks. Enumeration tools and wordlists can be used to discover files on TFTP. Files are not found via DNS TXT records (A), buffer overflows are not required (B), and ICMP is not used for file retrieval (D).

questions.question: What enumeration can the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) service be used for?

options.A: Enumerating SMB shares and Windows domain SIDs.
options.B: User enumeration (e.g., VRFY/EXPN/RCPT TO behavior), mail relay testing, and banner/version discovery.
options.C: Enumerating wireless networks and WPA handshakes.
options.D: Enumerating database tables via SQL injection.

questions.explanation: SMTP can be used for several enumeration techniques: VRFY (verify if a user exists), EXPN (expand a mailing list to reveal members), and RCPT TO (observing different response codes for valid vs invalid recipients to enumerate users). Banner grabbing reveals the mail server software and version. Open relay testing determines if the server forwards mail for unauthorized domains, which can be abused for spam or phishing. Tools like smtp-user-enum, nmap NSE scripts (smtp-enum-users, smtp-open-relay), and manual telnet/netcat connections are commonly used. SMTP cannot enumerate SMB shares (A), wireless networks (C), or database tables (D).

questions.question: What is steganography?

options.A: Hiding information within other data (e.g., images/audio) so the existence of the message is concealed.
options.B: Compressing files to reduce size for transmission.
options.C: Hashing passwords to store them securely.
options.D: Encrypting data so it is unreadable without a key.

questions.explanation: Steganography is the practice of hiding secret information within ordinary, non-secret data so that the very existence of the hidden message is concealed. Common carrier media include images (modifying least significant bits of pixel data), audio files, video, network traffic, or even text documents. Unlike encryption, which makes data unreadable but its presence obvious, steganography aims for undetectability — an observer should not suspect hidden content exists. It can be combined with encryption for defense in depth. Tools include steghide, OpenStego, and zsteg. It is not compression (B), not password hashing (C), and not encryption — though it is often used alongside encryption (D).

questions.question: What is a relative identifier (RID) Master?

options.A: An Active Directory FSMO role that allocates pools of RIDs to domain controllers so they can create unique SIDs for new objects.
options.B: A Kerberos server that issues ticket-granting tickets.
options.C: A DNS master server that handles zone transfers.
options.D: A Windows service that manages print queues across a forest.

questions.explanation: The RID Master is one of the five Active Directory FSMO (Flexible Single Master Operation) roles. It is responsible for allocating pools of Relative Identifiers (RIDs) to each domain controller in the domain. When a DC creates a new security principal (user, group, computer), it assigns a unique SID by combining the domain SID with a RID from its allocated pool. The RID Master ensures no two DCs issue the same RID, preventing SID collisions. If the RID Master is unavailable, DCs can continue creating objects only until their current RID pool is exhausted. It is not a Kerberos server (B), not a DNS server (C), and not related to print management (D).

questions.question: Explain Hashing functions ie MD5 and SHA1

options.A: They are public key algorithms used for key exchange.
options.B: They are compression algorithms used to shrink files.
options.C: They are symmetric ciphers used to encrypt disks.
options.D: They produce fixed-length digests for integrity; MD5 and SHA‑1 are considered collision-broken and unsuitable for modern security uses like signatures.

questions.explanation: Hash functions are one-way mathematical functions that take arbitrary input and produce a fixed-length output (digest): MD5 produces a 128-bit hash and SHA-1 produces a 160-bit hash. They are designed to be deterministic, fast to compute, irreversible, and collision-resistant. However, both MD5 and SHA-1 have been proven vulnerable to collision attacks — researchers have demonstrated practical collisions (e.g., SHAttered for SHA-1 in 2017, and numerous MD5 collisions). This means attackers can create two different inputs with the same hash, undermining integrity verification and digital signatures. Modern applications should use SHA-256 or SHA-3. They are not key exchange algorithms (A), not compression tools (B), and not symmetric ciphers (C).

questions.question: Explain with examples some protocols used for Wide Area Networks (WAN)

options.A: NFS, SMB, and AFP.
options.B: Examples include MPLS, PPP/PPPoE, Frame Relay (legacy), and BGP for interdomain routing.
options.C: WEP, WPA2, and WPA3.
options.D: USB, HDMI, and PCIe.

questions.explanation: WAN protocols facilitate communication over wide geographical areas: MPLS (Multi-Protocol Label Switching) provides efficient traffic engineering and QoS by routing packets using labels rather than IP lookups; PPP/PPPoE (Point-to-Point Protocol/over Ethernet) encapsulates network traffic for direct connections, commonly used by DSL providers; Frame Relay is a legacy packet-switched WAN technology largely replaced by MPLS; and BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the interdomain routing protocol that routes traffic between autonomous systems across the internet. NFS/SMB/AFP are file sharing protocols (A), WEP/WPA are wireless security protocols (C), and USB/HDMI/PCIe are physical hardware interfaces (D).

questions.question: What is a One-Time-Pad?

options.A: A public key certificate used to sign software.
options.B: A cipher using a truly random key as long as the message, used once; when used correctly it provides information-theoretic security.
options.C: A password policy requiring users to change passwords weekly.
options.D: A disk encryption mode that reuses the same key for all files.

questions.explanation: A One-Time Pad is a symmetric encryption technique where each bit or character of the plaintext is combined (typically XOR'd) with a corresponding bit or character from a truly random key that is at least as long as the message and used only once. When implemented correctly, it is the only cipher mathematically proven to be unbreakable (information-theoretic security, proven by Claude Shannon). However, practical challenges make it largely impractical: the key must be truly random (not pseudo-random), must be as long as the message, must never be reused (reuse enables key recovery via crib-dragging), and must be securely distributed to both parties. It is not a certificate (A), not a password policy (C), and reusing the key (as described in D) would completely break its security.

questions.question: What is a Schema Master?

options.A: A Windows service that manages DHCP leases.
options.B: A Kerberos role that stores user passwords in plaintext.
options.C: An Active Directory FSMO role that controls updates to the AD schema, ensuring only one DC processes schema modifications at a time.
options.D: A DNS role that authoritatively resolves all internet domains.

questions.explanation: The Schema Master is one of the five Active Directory FSMO roles and is unique across the entire forest (only one DC holds this role). It controls all modifications to the Active Directory schema — the blueprint that defines every object class and attribute available in AD (e.g., user objects, group objects, custom attributes). Only the Schema Master can write schema changes, ensuring consistency across all domain controllers in the forest. Schema modifications are needed when extending AD (e.g., for Exchange Server, SCCM, or custom applications). It is not a DHCP service (A), does not store passwords in plaintext (B), and is not a DNS role (D).

questions.question: Explain null sessions and restrict anonymous settings

options.A: Restrict anonymous settings disable all user authentication on a domain.
options.B: Null sessions occur only on Wi‑Fi networks using WEP.
options.C: Null sessions are encrypted TLS tunnels that improve privacy.
options.D: Null sessions are unauthenticated SMB connections that can expose information; restrict anonymous settings limit what anonymous users can enumerate over SMB/NetBIOS.

questions.explanation: Null sessions are unauthenticated connections to Windows SMB/CIFS shares and IPC$ (inter-process communication) endpoints using empty username and password. Historically (especially on older Windows versions), null sessions could enumerate significant information: user accounts, groups, shares, password policies, SIDs, and domain trusts via tools like enum4linux, rpcclient, and net use. The 'RestrictAnonymous' and 'RestrictAnonymousSAM' registry settings control what information anonymous users can enumerate. Setting RestrictAnonymous to 1 or 2 progressively limits anonymous enumeration. Modern Windows versions restrict null sessions by default, but misconfigurations are still found. Null sessions are not related to user authentication disabling (A), WEP (B), or TLS tunnels (C).

questions.question: What vulnerability might be present if Server Message Block (SMB) version 1 was enabled on a Windows device?

options.A: Exposure to legacy SMBv1 flaws and exploit chains (e.g., vulnerabilities leveraged by wormable attacks), plus weaker security features compared to SMBv2/v3.
options.B: It disables file sharing entirely, preventing any access.
options.C: It forces all traffic onto UDP, enabling amplification attacks only.
options.D: It automatically enables MFA for all users, which attackers can bypass.

questions.explanation: SMBv1 is an outdated protocol with numerous security vulnerabilities, most notably those exploited by EternalBlue (MS17-010), which was used by the WannaCry and NotPetya wormable ransomware attacks. SMBv1 lacks important security features present in later versions: SMBv2/v3 added improved signing, encryption (SMBv3), secure negotiation to prevent downgrade attacks, and pre-authentication integrity. Enabling SMBv1 exposes systems to remote code execution, information disclosure, and denial of service attacks. Microsoft recommends disabling SMBv1 via Group Policy or PowerShell (Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature). It does not disable file sharing (B), SMB uses TCP not UDP (C), and it has nothing to do with MFA (D).

questions.question: Explain the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model

options.A: A database normalization model for structuring tables.
options.B: A symmetric encryption model for key distribution.
options.C: A 7-layer conceptual model (Physical to Application) that standardizes how network functions are layered and interact.
options.D: A 3-layer model used only for cloud security.

questions.explanation: The OSI model defines seven layers: 1-Physical (electrical signals, cables), 2-Data Link (frames, MAC addresses, switches), 3-Network (packets, IP addressing, routing), 4-Transport (TCP/UDP, segments), 5-Session (session establishment/teardown), 6-Presentation (data formatting, encryption at this layer), and 7-Application (HTTP, DNS, SMTP). Each layer communicates with its peer layer on the remote system and provides services to the layer above. This model helps network professionals troubleshoot issues by layer, understand where security controls operate (e.g., firewalls at L3/L4, WAFs at L7), and design protocol stacks. It is not a database model (A), not an encryption model (B), and has 7 layers, not 3 (D).

questions.question: Explain the Department of Defense (DoD) networking model

options.A: A 4-layer model (Link, Internet, Transport, Application) similar to TCP/IP that describes network communications in broader layers.
options.B: A vulnerability scoring model used by CVSS.
options.C: A 7-layer model identical to OSI.
options.D: A wireless-only model for WPA authentication.

questions.explanation: The DoD (Department of Defense) model, also called the TCP/IP model, uses four layers instead of OSI's seven: 1-Link/Network Access (combines OSI Physical and Data Link — Ethernet, Wi-Fi), 2-Internet (equivalent to OSI Network — IP, ICMP, ARP), 3-Transport (equivalent to OSI Transport — TCP, UDP), and 4-Application (combines OSI Session, Presentation, Application — HTTP, DNS, FTP). It was developed alongside the ARPANET/internet protocols and is more practical for describing how TCP/IP networks actually operate. It is not a vulnerability scoring model (B), it has 4 layers not 7 (C), and it covers all network types, not just wireless (D).

questions.question: Explain how Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) works

options.A: It resolves domain names to IP addresses using recursive queries.
options.B: It authenticates users to a domain controller using tickets.
options.C: It encrypts network traffic between hosts using shared keys.
options.D: It automatically assigns IP configuration using a DORA process (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) and leases addresses for a period.

questions.explanation: DHCP dynamically assigns IP addresses and network configuration using the DORA process: the client broadcasts a Discover message, the server responds with an Offer containing an available IP, the client sends a Request for that IP, and the server confirms with an Acknowledge. Leases are time-limited, and clients must renew before expiry. DHCP also provides gateway, DNS server, domain name, and other options. Security concerns include rogue DHCP servers (MITM), DHCP starvation attacks (exhausting the address pool), and lack of authentication. Mitigations include DHCP snooping on switches and 802.1X. DNS resolution is a different protocol (A), Kerberos handles authentication (B), and DHCP does not encrypt traffic (C).

questions.question: What is a Start of Authority (SOA) record - with respect to Domain Name System (DNS)?

options.A: A DNS record that contains authoritative information about a zone, including the primary name server, admin contact, and serial/refresh timers.
options.B: A DNS record that indicates a mail exchanger for the domain.
options.C: A DNS record that maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.
options.D: A DNS record that stores a public key for DKIM signing.

questions.explanation: The SOA (Start of Authority) record is mandatory for every DNS zone and contains: the primary authoritative name server (MNAME), the responsible party's email address (RNAME), a serial number (incremented on zone changes to trigger transfers), and timing parameters — refresh interval (how often secondaries check for updates), retry interval (how long before retrying a failed refresh), expire time (when secondaries stop serving the zone if unreachable), and minimum TTL (negative caching duration). SOA records are essential for zone transfer synchronization between primary and secondary DNS servers. MX records handle mail routing (B), A records map hostnames to IPs (C), and DKIM keys are stored in TXT records (D).

questions.question: Explain what Domain Name System (DNS) is and explain how DNS works.

options.A: A protocol that assigns IP addresses dynamically to clients.
options.B: A transport protocol that provides reliable delivery over IP.
options.C: A firewall technology that blocks malicious domains by default.
options.D: A hierarchical naming system that maps domain names to records (A/AAAA/CNAME/MX, etc.) using recursive resolvers querying authoritative servers with caching.

questions.explanation: DNS is a hierarchical, distributed naming system that translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses and other records. The resolution process involves: a client stub resolver sending a query to a recursive resolver, which queries the root name servers, then TLD (top-level domain) servers, then authoritative name servers for the specific domain. Results are cached at each level based on TTL values to reduce load. Record types include A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (name server), TXT (text data), PTR (reverse lookup), and SOA (zone authority). Security concerns include DNS spoofing/poisoning, cache poisoning, zone transfer leakage, and DNS tunneling; DNSSEC adds cryptographic integrity. DNS does not assign IPs dynamically — that is DHCP (A), it is not a transport protocol (B), and it does not block domains by default (C).

questions.question: Explain the IP protocol and explain IP addresses.

options.A: IP routes packets across networks using source/destination IP addresses; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.
options.B: IP encrypts packets end-to-end by default.
options.C: IP addresses are MAC addresses formatted with colons.
options.D: IP is an application-layer protocol for web pages.

questions.explanation: IP (Internet Protocol) is a Layer 3 (network layer) protocol responsible for routing packets across interconnected networks using source and destination IP addresses. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses (e.g., 192.168.1.1), providing approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (e.g., 2001:db8::1), vastly expanding the address space. IP provides connectionless, best-effort delivery — it does not guarantee delivery, ordering, or integrity (those are handled by upper-layer protocols like TCP). Key header fields include TTL (time to live), protocol number, and source/destination addresses. IP does not encrypt by default — IPsec is needed for that (B). IP addresses are not MAC addresses (C). IP operates at the network layer, not the application layer (D).

questions.question: Explain Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)

options.A: A protocol that replaces TCP with a faster transport.
options.B: A method of IP addressing and routing using variable-length prefixes (e.g., /24) to allocate and aggregate address space efficiently.
options.C: A technique to hide web traffic inside DNS queries.
options.D: A Wi‑Fi security standard that supersedes WPA3.

questions.explanation: CIDR replaced the rigid classful addressing system (Class A/B/C) with variable-length subnet masking using prefix notation (e.g., /24 = 256 addresses, /16 = 65,536 addresses). This allows organizations to receive precisely sized address blocks rather than wasteful class-based allocations, significantly improving IPv4 address efficiency. CIDR also enables route aggregation (supernetting) — multiple contiguous networks can be advertised as a single route, reducing routing table size. For example, four /24 networks can be aggregated into a single /22. It is not a transport protocol (A), not related to DNS tunneling (C), and not a Wi-Fi standard (D).

questions.question: Explain how Machine-in-the-Middle (MITM) techniques work with the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP).

options.A: By changing BGP routes on the public internet without access to the LAN.
options.B: By exploiting DNSSEC signatures to change records.
options.C: By brute forcing WPA passwords over the air.
options.D: By poisoning ARP caches so victims map an IP to the attacker’s MAC, allowing interception/relay of traffic on a LAN segment.

questions.explanation: ARP MITM attacks exploit the fact that ARP has no authentication mechanism. An attacker on the same LAN segment sends unsolicited (gratuitous) ARP replies to the victim and the gateway, associating the attacker's MAC address with the other party's IP address in each device's ARP cache. This causes traffic between the victim and gateway to flow through the attacker, who can then intercept, modify, or forward it (relay). Tools like arpspoof, Ettercap, and Bettercap automate this attack. Mitigations include: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches, DHCP snooping (which DAI relies on for trusted bindings), static ARP entries for critical systems, port security, and using encrypted protocols (TLS/SSH) to protect data even if intercepted. BGP attacks are internet-scale routing attacks (A), DNSSEC is unrelated (B), and WPA cracking targets wireless, not ARP (C).

questions.question: What is the function of Port Address Translation (PAT)?

options.A: To allocate DNS zones to authoritative servers.
options.B: To allow many internal hosts to share a single public IP by translating internal addresses/ports to external ports (a form of NAT).
options.C: To route packets based on MAC addresses only.
options.D: To encrypt TCP ports so scanners cannot detect services.

questions.explanation: Port Address Translation (PAT), also called NAT overload, is a form of Network Address Translation that allows multiple internal hosts (using private RFC 1918 addresses) to share a single public IP address by mapping each session to a unique source port number on the public IP. The NAT device maintains a translation table tracking internal IP:port to external IP:port mappings. This conserves public IPv4 addresses and provides a degree of obscurity for internal network topology (though it is not a security control). PAT is the most common form of NAT used in home and enterprise internet gateways. It does not allocate DNS zones (A), does not operate on MAC addresses alone (C), and does not encrypt ports (D).

questions.question: What is the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)?

options.A: A file transfer protocol that runs only over UDP.
options.B: A time synchronization protocol for network devices.
options.C: A protocol for accessing and managing directory services (e.g., Active Directory), used for querying users, groups, and objects.
options.D: A routing protocol that selects paths between routers.

questions.explanation: LDAP is an application-layer protocol (TCP ports 389 for plaintext, 636 for LDAPS/TLS) used to query and modify directory services — hierarchical databases storing information about users, groups, computers, and other network objects. Active Directory is the most common LDAP-based directory. LDAP uses a tree structure (Distinguished Names like CN=John,OU=Users,DC=example,DC=com) and supports operations like search, bind (authenticate), add, modify, and delete. Security concerns include: cleartext LDAP binds transmitting credentials, anonymous binds leaking directory information, LDAP injection, and overly permissive ACLs. Mitigations include enforcing LDAPS or STARTTLS, disabling anonymous binds, and applying least-privilege access. LDAP is not a file transfer protocol (A), not for time sync (B), and not a routing protocol (D).

questions.question: Name and explain two distance vector routing protocols

options.A: RIP and EIGRP (often treated as advanced DV): they exchange route information with neighbors based on distance/metric rather than full topology.
options.B: ARP and ICMP; they compute shortest paths across WANs.
options.C: OSPF and IS‑IS; they are distance vector protocols.
options.D: BGP and HTTP; they exchange routes over the web.

questions.explanation: Distance vector routing protocols share routing information with directly connected neighbors based on metrics (e.g., hop count, composite metrics). RIP (Routing Information Protocol) uses hop count as its metric (maximum 15 hops), sends periodic full updates every 30 seconds, and is simple but slow to converge. EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) is Cisco's advanced distance vector protocol using a composite metric (bandwidth, delay, reliability, load) with DUAL algorithm for loop-free, fast convergence and supports incremental updates. Distance vector protocols are susceptible to routing loops (mitigated by split horizon, route poisoning, holddown timers). OSPF and IS-IS are link-state protocols, not distance vector (C). ARP/ICMP are not routing protocols (B). BGP is a path-vector protocol and HTTP is not a routing protocol (D).

questions.question: Explain Medium Access Control (MAC) addresses and explain what an Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) is?

options.A: A MAC is an IP address; an OUI is the DNS zone name.
options.B: A MAC is a port number; an OUI is a routing metric.
options.C: A MAC is a Layer 2 hardware address; the OUI is the first 24 bits identifying the manufacturer (or assignment) of the network interface.
options.D: A MAC is a user ID; an OUI is a password hash.

questions.explanation: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a 48-bit Layer 2 hardware identifier assigned to network interface cards, typically displayed as six pairs of hexadecimal digits (e.g., AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF). The first 24 bits (first three octets) form the OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier), assigned by IEEE to manufacturers — for example, 00:50:56 identifies VMware, and DC:A6:32 identifies Raspberry Pi. The remaining 24 bits are assigned by the manufacturer to uniquely identify each device. OUI lookups are useful during penetration testing and network reconnaissance to identify device manufacturers and types. Modern devices may use MAC address randomization for privacy. MACs are not IP addresses (A), not port numbers (B), and not user IDs (D).

questions.question: What is firewalking (with respect to network security)?

options.A: A technique for exploiting SQL injection to enumerate tables.
options.B: A technique to infer firewall rules by sending packets with crafted TTL values to determine which ports/protocols are permitted through a filtering device.
options.C: A physical security test of sprinkler systems and fire doors.
options.D: A method to crack WPA2 by capturing handshakes.

questions.explanation: Firewalking is a reconnaissance technique that determines which ports and protocols are permitted through a firewall or packet filter. It works by sending packets with TTL values set to expire one hop past the firewall — if the firewall permits the traffic, the packet reaches the next hop and generates an ICMP Time Exceeded response, confirming the port is open through the filter. If the firewall blocks the traffic, no response is received. Tools like firewalk and hping3 automate this technique. First, a traceroute determines the hop count to the firewall, then probes are sent with TTL = hop_count + 1. It is not related to SQL injection (A), physical fire safety (C), or WPA2 cracking (D).

questions.question: Explain the Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) protocol

options.A: A file transfer protocol used for downloading firmware.
options.B: A wireless security standard improving on WEP; WPA uses TKIP (legacy) and WPA2 uses AES-CCMP, while WPA3 further improves key exchange and protection.
options.C: A routing protocol for exchanging routes between autonomous systems.
options.D: An email authentication method based on DNS TXT records.

questions.explanation: WPA was developed as an interim replacement for WEP, using TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) with RC4 cipher and per-packet key mixing to address WEP's key reuse flaws. WPA2 replaced TKIP with AES-CCMP (Counter Mode CBC-MAC Protocol), providing significantly stronger encryption and integrity protection — it has been mandatory for Wi-Fi certification since 2006. WPA3 further improves security with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replacing the PSK 4-way handshake, providing forward secrecy and resistance to offline dictionary attacks, plus mandatory Protected Management Frames (PMF). Enterprise modes (WPA2/3-Enterprise) use 802.1X/RADIUS for per-user authentication. WPA is not a file transfer protocol (A), not a routing protocol (C), and not an email authentication method (D).

questions.question: Explain IPSec

options.A: A DNS protocol that ensures integrity of DNS records.
options.B: A suite that secures IP traffic with authentication and encryption using AH/ESP, often for VPNs, operating in transport or tunnel mode.
options.C: A TCP option that increases window size for performance.
options.D: A web application firewall that blocks SQL injection.

questions.explanation: IPsec is a suite of protocols operating at the network layer (Layer 3) that provides security for IP communications. It uses two main protocols: AH (Authentication Header) for integrity and authentication without encryption, and ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) for confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. IPsec operates in two modes: transport mode (protects the payload, used for host-to-host) and tunnel mode (encapsulates the entire IP packet, used for VPNs). IKE (Internet Key Exchange) handles the negotiation of Security Associations (SAs) and key exchange. IPsec is widely used for site-to-site VPNs, remote-access VPNs, and securing routing protocols. It is not a DNS protocol — DNSSEC is (A), not a TCP option (C), and not a WAF (D).

questions.question: Where would you find the hosts file and what is its purpose?

options.A: It is stored only on DNS servers and defines authoritative zones.
options.B: It is stored in the browser cache and defines TLS certificates.
options.C: It is stored in the router firmware and defines NAT rules.
options.D: It is a local name-to-IP mapping file (e.g., /etc/hosts on Unix-like systems; %SystemRoot%\System32\drivers\etc\hosts on Windows) that overrides DNS resolution.

questions.explanation: The hosts file is a local plain-text file that maps hostnames to IP addresses, consulted before DNS resolution in most OS configurations. On Unix/Linux/macOS it is located at /etc/hosts; on Windows at %SystemRoot%\System32\drivers\etc\hosts. Entries follow the format 'IP_address hostname' (e.g., '127.0.0.1 localhost'). The hosts file can be used legitimately for local development, ad blocking, or overriding DNS for testing. Malware may modify the hosts file to redirect legitimate domains to malicious IPs (pharming) or block security update servers. It is not stored on DNS servers (A), not in browser cache (B), and not in router firmware (C). Protecting the hosts file with appropriate file permissions is a basic hardening step.

questions.question: Explain how Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANS) work

options.A: VLANs are Layer 3 routing protocols that replace IP.
options.B: VLANs encrypt Wi‑Fi frames so attackers cannot sniff traffic.
options.C: VLANs logically segment Layer 2 networks by tagging frames (802.1Q) so devices can be separated into distinct broadcast domains on the same physical infrastructure.
options.D: VLANs are only for connecting remote sites over the internet.

questions.explanation: VLANs logically segment a physical network into separate broadcast domains at Layer 2 using IEEE 802.1Q tagging. Each VLAN has a unique ID (1-4094) inserted into the Ethernet frame header on trunk ports. Devices in the same VLAN can communicate at Layer 2, but traffic between VLANs requires a Layer 3 router or Layer 3 switch (inter-VLAN routing), where ACLs and firewall rules can control cross-VLAN access.
